replies.author: TheReviewerWildTake
replies.body:
Tbh it worked a bit differently at that time, because in 20xx we knew what was the level of graphics in games at that point.   
  
No one watched 2004 WoW cinematics and thought "oh, this is how it is gonna look in the game", since we were coming from other MMOs, from Warcraft , Starcraft etc , and everyone knew that OG blizzard were good with their trailers (unlike modern day blizztards and their lame flower sniffing videos :D )   
  
In those days it was simple - people with money made custom cinematics, companies with low budgets used in-game engine.

However, when we were in 90-ies, I remember being pissed off about the fact that my console\`s cartridge had all the cool visuals on it, promising epic adventures with ultra realistic heroes, and then you had to play some blocky cube-dude with some basic 'pew-pew' gameplay :D 



Today we are bombarded by ads that use misleading trailers of epic battles and coolness and stuff  and then gameplay is worse version of tetris...

So maybe it is not even the gap between "cinematics visuals vs gameplay visuals" per se , but rather specific time period we are in, when there is a lot of bait and switch games around.

BUT! tbh I don\`t think your trailer is that misleading. Seems that even combat skill visuals are quite aligned with trailer. And it is easy to connect the dots who is who, and what it meant to represent.  
  
I think the problem people are trying to articulate, is that due to AI style, it looks like with those games that do bait and switch. But I don\`t think it applies to your game. Yet, this is "the current year", so have to adapt... 

I agree with the statement that it is way too long and too flashy for MMO work-in-progress intro, simply because at this point people just want to have answer "why play this, and not other MMOs", "what fun systems are in this game", "how is combat", "are there guilds", "is it PVP or PVE" etc.  
  
Also your trailer is leaning heavily into combat, but does not explain what is this place, what is going on, who is attacking whom etc.  
In 2004 WoW cinematics we had advantage on knowing what is this world and why these dudes are fighting.  
You may look at games that release their first installment and see how they present their world.  
  
There is also no hook in your trailer, because at this point people don\`t care that one AI dude fights another AI dude. They have no feelings towards them, and have no idea what is going and why they have to care.  
You need to introduce characters and their world first a bit (with AI or without it) .

replies.author: Fun_Bumblebee_3978
replies.body:
Honestly, this is one of the best comments I've gotten on this whole post, so thank you for taking the time to write it.

The 90s cartridge thing made me laugh because I lived that exact betrayal: box art promising a legendary warrior, and then you're controlling three pixels with an attitude. And you're right that today it's worse, because now the bait and switch comes with a budget.

I'll be straight with you: I'm not a marketing expert. I'm a developer who tried to show a bit of everything at once, some visuals, some story, some gameplay, and ended up showing none of them properly. Like trying to explain a whole movie in a 10-second voice note.

Your point about the hook really landed. People don't care about two guys fighting if they don't know who they are or why they're fighting. And the questions you listed, why this and not another MMO, what systems it has, how combat feels, guilds, PvP or PvE, that's exactly what someone looking at an MMO in development wants answered first. Not fireworks.

So I already reworked it. The new video is full gameplay: the survival side, the hardcore part where dying actually costs you, and some of the crafting systems. Less cinematic, more "this is what you'll actually be doing." Presenting the world and its characters properly is next on the list, and your comment gave me a good starting point for that.

Here's the new gameplay video if you want to take a look: 

https://reddit.com/link/pbbjj2c/video/sgkab1r6t0rh1/player

Thanks again. Criticism like this is worth more than a hundred upvotes.

replies.author: Fun_Bumblebee_3978
replies.body:
Thanks for asking, genuinely. Here's the long version.

I've been a developer for about 10 years, and a gamer for much longer than that. I'm also a graphic designer, and basically a full-stack dev in whatever language the problem demands. If I don't know it, I learn it. Before Ashram, that was my entire life: code by day, games by night, and the occasional existential crisis about why nobody makes MMOs like the old ones anymore.

At 33, I finally stopped complaining and started building. Turns out complaining is a lot cheaper.

Like a lot of you, I was drowning in nostalgia for a good MMORPG. So I took an old game I used to play years ago as a starting point and rebuilt the story my own way, keeping it coherent, but making it mine. Same soul, new body.

Now, the honest part: I said 6 months in the post, and that's true, but it's not the whole story. I actually started about 7 years ago. On and off. Very off. I'd start something, build it with all the passion in the world, and then abandon it for five months, sometimes a year, like a gym membership in February. Over those years I kept buying assets little by little, the way some people collect stamps, except stamps don't need rigging.

What changed was the tools. With what's available today, working solo feels less like being one guy and more like having a battalion behind me. AI doesn't do the work for me, it multiplies what I can already do. It's the difference between digging with a spoon and digging with an excavator: you still have to know where to dig, and you still have to show up every day.

So yes: 7 years of trying, 6 months of actually doing. Everything before that was a very long tutorial.

That's my story. Thanks again for asking, and for asking instead of assuming. That already puts you ahead of half this thread.

replies.author: Fun_Bumblebee_3978
replies.body:
Thanks, man! And welcome to the club. The pay is terrible, the hours are worse, and somehow we all keep signing up.

It really depends on what you're building, and I'd be happy to help, more than a hand if you need it. But here are a few things I wish someone had told me before I started:

**Don't panic when people criticize your work.** And they will. As you can see from this very thread, some people will review your game without opening it, the way some people review restaurants from the parking lot. Take the criticism that's useful, and let the rest slide off like rain on a window. Some of the harshest comments here actually made my game better. The others just made my afternoon longer.

**When you feel overwhelmed, keep pushing.** Game dev is like climbing a mountain where the summit moves every time you look up. You'll fix one bug and three more will show up to the funeral. That's normal. Progress doesn't feel like progress while you're in it, it only looks like progress when you look back.

**And when you want to quit, don't quit. Take a break instead.** Go for a walk, sleep, touch some grass, play someone else's game for a while. Your brain keeps solving problems when you're not looking, it's like leaving dough to rise. I spent years starting and abandoning this project before I learned that resting and giving up are two very different things.

Then come back with energy and give it your best. Consistency beats talent, and it absolutely destroys motivation, which shows up whenever it feels like it, like a cat.

What are you working on? Genre, engine, solo or team? Tell me more and I'll give you something more specific than fortune-cookie wisdom.

And thanks for giving Ashram a try. If you find bugs, consider it professional networking.
